newsitem.title: USA: Japan welcomes G7 forex remarks, signal intervention.
newsitem.headline: Japan welcomes G7 forex remarks, signal intervention.

text.p: Japan on Sunday welcomed the outcome of a Group of Seven meeting whose final statement suggests that the group opposes an excessive fall of the yen, and it signaled that it will take action to make sure the intention is carried out.

After five hours of talks, finance ministers and central bankers of the G7 nations issued a statement that stipulates they oppose currency volatility and that they would act against such moves as needed.
The G7 groups Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

Given repeated warnings of U.S. officials against a resurgence of Japan's trade surplus, Tokyo has expressed strong concern about the recent weakness of the yen, which could help boost Japan's exports by making Japanese goods more competitive in world markets and thus push up its trade surplus.
Japan's trade surplus with the United States has been rising over the past six months from year-earlier levels. It rose 11.2 percent in March to $3.04 billion.

Rekindling of trade friction with the United States -- Japan's major trading partner -- as a result of a sharp increase in the external surplus could hurt Japanese companies by forcing Washington to restrain Japan's exports.
"Japan's concern about excessive yen weakness was clearly reflected in the G7 statement," said an international monetary source who asked for anonymity.
The source added the intention of the G7 will become clear from action by monetary authorities of the G7 countries.
Ignoring the intention, the dollar rose nearly one yen to 127.10 yen in early trading on Monday in Tokyo.
"Japan is satisfied with the outcome of the G7 regarding exchange rates," said a senior Japanese government official.
It is not clear if all G7 countries will intervene in currency markets to prevent a further rise of the dollar, but at least the United States appeared to side with Japan.

In a meeting between Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin prior to the G7 meeting, Mitsuzuka voiced concern about the yen's recent movement and Rubin shared the Japanese concern.

The United States appeared to have softened its stance against Japan's fiscal policy which U.S. officials have said entails risks of slowing economic growth, pushing up its external surplus and stimulating protectionist moves in the United States.
In the bilateral meeting, Rubin welcomed Japan's commitment to economic deregulation and the steps it had taken to promote financial reform.

The G7 statement also noted Japan's efforts on financial reforms by saying, "Further structural reform, including broader deregulation initiatives and appropriate fiscal structural reforms, are important over the medium term to revitalize the Japanese economy further."

Mitsuzuka has said Japan cannot afford to take any fiscal measures -- one of the effective steps to prop up the economy -- as the nation's budget defict has now soared to the largest among G7 countries.

Instead, Japan maintains that its structural reforms in various areas, including fiscal, economic and administrative systems, will over the long term create new business opportunities and stimulate the economy.
